title: Impact of Indoor Smoking Ban on Respiratory Health

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
I will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of indoor smoking bans on respiratory hospital admissions. The method compares the change in outcomes before and after the ban implementation between treated municipalities (with the ban) and control municipalities (without the ban). The key assumption is parallel trends: in the absence of treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trend in respiratory hospital admissions.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s36_data.csv")

# Display basic summary statistics
cat("=== BASIC SUMMARY STATISTICS ===\n")
summary(data)

# Check balance of treatment assignment
cat("\n=== TREATMENT ASSIGNMENT BALANCE ===\n")
table(data$treated, data$post)

# Main DID regression
cat("\n=== MAIN DID REGRESSION ===\n")
did_model <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)

# Use robust standard errors
robust_se <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1")))
coef_summary <- summary(did_model)$coefficients
coef_summary[, 2] <- robust_se
coef_summary[, 3] <- coef_summary[, 1] / robust_se
coef_summary[, 4] <- 2 * pt(-abs(coef_summary[, 3]), df = did_model$df.residual)

print(coef_summary)

# Extract and display the main treatment effect
treatment_effect <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
cat(sprintf("\nTREATMENT EFFECT: %.4f\n", treatment_effect))
cat(sprintf("This represents a %.2f%% change in hospital admissions\n", 
            (exp(treatment_effect) - 1) * 100))

# Robustness check 1: Include unit fixed effects
cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 1: UNIT FIXED EFFECTS ===\n")
did_fe <- lm(y ~ factor(unit_id) + post + treat_x_post, data = data)
fe_effect <- coef(did_fe)["treat_x_post"]
cat(sprintf("Treatment effect with unit FE: %.4f\n", fe_effect))

# Robustness check 2: Include time fixed effects
cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 2: TIME FIXED EFFECTS ===\n")
did_time_fe <- lm(y ~ treated + factor(period) + treat_x_post, data = data)
time_fe_effect <- coef(did_time_fe)["treat_x_post"]
cat(sprintf("Treatment effect with time FE: %.4f\n", time_fe_effect))

# Robustness check 3: Two-way fixed effects
cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 3: TWO-WAY FIXED EFFECTS ===\n")
did_twfe <- lm(y ~ factor(unit_id) + factor(period) + treat_x_post, data = data)
twfe_effect <- coef(did_twfe)["treat_x_post"]
twfe_robust_se <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(did_twfe, type = "HC1")))["treat_x_post"]
twfe_t_stat <- twfe_effect / twfe_robust_se
twfe_p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(twfe_t_stat), df = did_twfe$df.residual)

cat(sprintf("Treatment effect with two-way FE: %.4f\n", twfe_effect))
cat(sprintf("Robust standard error: %.4f\n", twfe_robust_se))
cat(sprintf("t-statistic: %.4f\n", twfe_t_stat))
cat(sprintf("p-value: %.4f\n", twfe_p_value))

# Check for parallel trends (pre-treatment comparison)
cat("\n=== PARALLEL TRENDS CHECK ===\n")
pre_treatment <- data[data$post == 0, ]
if(nrow(pre_treatment) > 0) {
  pre_trend_test <- lm(y ~ treated * period, data = pre_treatment)
  interaction_coef <- coef(pre_trend_test)["treated:period"]
  cat(sprintf("Pre-treatment trend difference: %.4f\n", interaction_coef))
  if(abs(interaction_coef) < 0.05) {
    cat("Parallel trends assumption likely satisfied\n")
  } else {
    cat("WARNING: Potential violation of parallel trends\n")
  }
}

# Final summary
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULTS SUMMARY ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Main DID estimate: %.4f\n", treatment_effect))
cat(sprintf("Two-way FE estimate: %.4f\n", twfe_effect))
cat(sprintf("Percentage change in admissions: %.2f%%\n", (exp(treatment_effect) - 1) * 100))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a negative coefficient on the treat_x_post interaction term, indicating that indoor smoking bans reduce respiratory hospital admissions. The magnitude should be around -0.15 to -0.30 in log terms, representing approximately a 15-25% reduction in hospital admissions. This expectation is based on public health literature showing that smoking bans reduce exposure to secondhand smoke, leading to improved respiratory health outcomes. The effect should be statistically significant and robust across different specifications, supporting the causal interpretation that indoor smoking bans improve public health by reducing respiratory illnesses requiring hospitalization.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in respiratory illness admissions over time between municipalities with and without the ban.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The indoor smoking ban is associated with an increase in hospital admissions for respiratory illnesses.
